walkthroughs.body_html:
Newtonian World & Astrophysics — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Newtonian World & Astrophysics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Newtonian World & Astrophysics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A star with surface temperature twice that of the Sun emits how many times more power per unit area?
Wien's law allows us to determine a star's:
options: Distance
Surface temperature
Mass
Radial velocity

mcqs.q: Why do brighter-looking stars not necessarily have higher luminosity?
options: Apparent brightness depends on both luminosity and distance — a closer dim star can look brighter than a distant luminous one.
Brighter-looking stars are always intrinsically more luminous.
Apparent brightness depends only on the star's temperature.
Light-years — it's a measure of cosmic distance.

mcqs.q: What does the cosmological redshift of distant galaxies indicate?
options: Space itself is expanding, stretching the wavelength of light from distant galaxies as it travels.
The galaxies are turning red because they are getting older.
Galaxies are moving through space away from us, like objects flying outward from a centre.
Light-years — it's a measure of cosmic distance.

mcqs.q: What are typical units for the Hubble constant?
options: Metres per second — it's the speed at which the universe expands.
km per second per megaparsec (km/s/Mpc) — recession speed per unit distance.
Light-years — it's a measure of cosmic distance.
Apparent brightness depends only on the star's temperature.
